english: So we must understand “after the blow” not as the time after the blow stopped, but as the time after it began. After the fourteen years of illness, he lived another one hundred fifty years. Since the years of his former prosperity were seventy-eight, the doubled time of his later good fortune comes to one hundred fifty years. When the fourteen years of the blow are added, the total is one hundred seventy years, and that is how the Scripture finds that he lived one hundred seventy years after the blow—that is, from the time the blow was brought upon him. In this way the double repayment of his abundance is also preserved. To sum up, then, you will count as follows: he lived in wealth and good children seventy-eight years; in the loss of everything and the affliction of the body fourteen years; in the second good fortune one hundred fifty-seven years. So the whole time of his life was two hundred forty-eight years, as the sacred book about him says.

Verse 17. And Job died an old man and full of days. It is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises. Aquila and Symmachus came and brought the book to an end, as if following the Hebrew. Theodotion, however, ends it with the Seventy, lacking nothing—no time, no life. It is written again that he will rise with those whom the Lord raises, meaning the righteous. For the ungodly, it says, will not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous (Psalm 1:5). We accept these words too, even if they are not of the whole texture, but at least as woven into the book by one of the saints. Nevertheless, we accept them all, having received the book in this way from the fathers.

Verse 18. This name is interpreted from the Syriac book. He now calls the Hebrew dialect Syriac, since many also call Judea Syria and the Palestinians Syrians. And Herodotus the historian says: “The Indians, Egyptians, Arabians, and the Syrians in Palestine are circumcised.” That is what they call the Jews.
